threshold_policy: Hypotheses only; preregister and validate before operational use

sections.text:
This document explains what moves the Nasdaq-100, when professionals trade it, and when they stand aside. It cannot give you a strategy with a proven edge, and nothing here is a prediction of profit. Real money is at risk, so the default answer in this document is always NO TRADE unless every gate passes.

**Why training your AI has been hard.** Index direction over minutes to hours is mostly noise, and the rules that work change with the regime. A model fed raw candles learns the last regime, not the market. Professionals do the opposite: they decide first whether the market is tradable at all (events, volatility, liquidity, spread), and only then look for a setup. The AI should be built the same way, as a stack of filters with a small, well-tested trigger at the end.

**The market you are about to trade is not a normal one.** As of 6 November 2026 the Nasdaq-100 had its worst day since April 2025 (about -6.3% on 5 November, per one live report), volatility spiked, and the Fed is being priced to raise rates. Section 3 and section 8 explain what that means for sizing and for which strategies are even allowed. Treat the first weeks after a shock like this as the highest-risk period, not the best opportunity.

**How to use this with your code agent.** Sections 2 to 10 are knowledge: what drives the index and why. Sections 11 to 14 are decisions: the order of checks, risk limits, and the no-trade list. Section 15 turns it into data fields and rules. Every number marked *approximate* needs confirming against your broker or the cited source before it goes into code.

**Evidence labels used throughout.** *Sourced* means I opened the page and it is linked. *Convention* means widely used practice with no strong proof it earns money. *Hypothesis* means a plausible idea your backtests must test before you trust it.

NAS100, US100 and USTECH100 are broker names for the same thing: a contract that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index (ticker NDX), the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on Nasdaq. Your symbol `USTECH100M` is a broker-specific CFD on it, not the index itself and not the futures contract.

**How the index is built** ([Nasdaq NDX methodology](https://indexes.nasdaqomx.com/docs/methodology_NDX.pdf), *sourced*):

- Modified market-cap weighted, so the largest companies move it most.
- Excludes financial companies (banks, insurers). That is why it behaves as a technology and growth index.
- Capped at 24% for any one company (reduced to 20% at rebalance), and companies above 4.5% may not total 48% or more (reduced to 40%). A special rebalance can be triggered if these are breached at the close.
- The index is calculated on U.S. market days and published once per second from 09:30:01 to 17:16:00 ET.
- Annual reconstitution is effective at the open on the first trading day after the third Friday in December; quarterly rebalances take effect after the third Friday of March, June and September.

**What this means for trading.**

1. A handful of mega-cap stocks decide most days. When two or three of them move together, the index moves with them, and nothing about "market structure" on the chart tells you why.
2. The index is a bet on growth stocks and long-duration cash flows, so it is more sensitive to interest rates than the S&P 500 or the Dow.
3. Rebalance and reconstitution days add flows unrelated to news. The third Friday of March, June, September and December is also options and futures expiry ("quad witching"), which distorts volume and the close.

**Three instruments, one underlying.** Use the right one for the right job.

| Instrument | What it is | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NDX | The cash index, calculated 09:30 to 17:16 ET | Reference level only; you cannot trade it directly |
| Nasdaq-100 futures (NQ, MNQ) | Exchange-traded, almost 24 hours on weekdays | Price discovery overnight, true volume, and the market's real opening gap |
| Broker CFD (`USTECH100M`) | Broker's quote derived from futures or cash, with its own spread, swap and hours | The only thing you actually trade; costs and gaps are the broker's, not the index's |

The CFD can differ from the index in three ways your code must handle: a spread that widens when the market is thin, a different timestamp convention (section 6), and a daily break when the broker stops quoting. See section 13.

sections.section: 3. Macro drivers and where they stand now
sections.text:
The Nasdaq-100 is priced mainly off interest rates and growth expectations. When the market expects higher rates for longer, future profits are worth less today, and long-duration growth stocks fall the most. That is the single most useful sentence for reading this index.

**Where things stand (early November 2026).** These are reported conditions, not forecasts, and some figures conflict between outlets.

| Driver | Latest reported state | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fed policy rate | 3.75% to 4.00%, after a 0.25 point hike on 16 Sep 2026, the first in more than three years. Held on 28 Oct by 10 to 2, with two governors dissenting in favour of a hike | [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/fed-rate-hike-warsh-trump-inflation/), [The National](https://www.thenationalnews.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/federal-reserve-decision-interest-rates/) |
| Fed chair | Kevin Warsh, who said inflation "is too high, and has been for too long" | [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/fed-rate-hike-warsh-trump-inflation/) |
| Next decision | 9 Dec 2026, 2:00 pm ET. Futures priced a December hike at about 78%, up from 70%, after the jobs report | [CP24](https://www.cp24.com/news/money/2026/11/06/nasdaq-eyes-higher-open-as-chips-pare-losses-rate-hike-fears-linger/) |
| Inflation | CPI 2.4% (Jan), 4.2% (May, three-year high), 3.4% (Aug). Energy CPI up 20.4% over 12 months to September | [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/fed-rate-hike-warsh-trump-inflation/), [The National](https://www.thenationalnews.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/federal-reserve-decision-interest-rates/) |
| 10-year Treasury yield | Near 5%; closed at 5.08% on 15 Oct | [The National](https://www.thenationalnews.com/business/economy/2026/10/28/federal-reserve-decision-interest-rates/), [CME Group](https://www.cmegroup.com/videos/2026/10/15/10-year-treasury-yield-posts-biggest-two-day-drop-of-2026-10-15.html) |
| Oil | Iran war cut Gulf supply; crude above $100 earlier. On 6 Nov WTI about $90.6, Brent about $98.2 | [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/fed-rate-hike-warsh-trump-inflation/), [TheStreet](https://www.thestreet.com/stock-market-today/stock-market-today-dow-jones-sp-500-nasdaq-updates-nov-06-2026) |
| Jobs | October payrolls +165,000 versus 59,000 expected; unemployment 4.1% (the same page also says 4.2% was forecast) | [TheStreet](https://www.thestreet.com/stock-market-today/stock-market-today-dow-jones-sp-500-nasdaq-updates-nov-06-2026) |
| Volatility | VIX jumped by the most in about 19 months on 5 Nov, then eased to 26.70 on 6 Nov | [CP24](https://www.cp24.com/news/money/2026/11/06/nasdaq-eyes-higher-open-as-chips-pare-losses-rate-hike-fears-linger/) |

**How each driver reaches the index.**

- **Fed and real yields.** A hawkish surprise raises yields, which cuts the value of distant profits. The reaction is often fastest in the Nasdaq-100 within minutes of the 2:00 pm ET statement and again at the 2:30 pm press conference.
- **Inflation prints (CPI, PPI, PCE).** In a hiking cycle, a hot print means a higher chance of a hike, so good economic news can be bad for the index. In this regime a strong jobs number was followed by higher hike odds and a tech selloff.
- **Jobs report.** Moves both growth and rate expectations, so the sign of the reaction depends on the regime. Do not hard-code "strong jobs equals up".
- **Treasury yields and the dollar.** Fast rises in the 10-year yield are the usual source of pressure on growth stocks, and the effect looks stronger when yields are already high (section 9). A strong dollar hurts overseas revenue of the mega-caps.
- **Oil and geopolitics.** Oil feeds inflation, which feeds Fed hikes. War headlines (Strait of Hormuz, strikes, talks) arrive at any hour and can gap the index.
- **Politics and regulation.** On 5 Nov, midterm results in data-centre states raised fears of tougher AI regulation and slower data-centre build-out, and chips led the fall (section 4).

**The closest historical parallel is 2022**, when the Fed raised rates and the index fell about 34.8% from peak to trough within the year (ChartRow estimate using QQQ as a proxy). That is a pattern to respect, not a forecast.

**Agent rule.** Store each of these as a daily regime input (policy rate, hike probability, 10-year yield and its 5-day change, oil, VIX, dollar index). Use them to restrict risk, never to generate a buy or sell on their own.

sections.section: 4. Mega-cap concentration and the AI trade
sections.text:
A few stocks decide the index, and right now they are mostly one theme: artificial-intelligence spending. When that theme reverses, the whole index moves with it, whatever the chart looked like beforehand.

**How concentrated it is.** On 13 Feb 2026 the top ten holdings added up to about 47% of the Invesco QQQ fund (which tracks the index): Nvidia 8.75%, Apple 7.44%, Microsoft 5.87%, Amazon 4.18%, Tesla 4.10%, Meta 3.70%, Walmart 3.56%, Alphabet (two share classes) 6.76%, Broadcom 3.02% ([StockAnalysis](https://www.stockanalysis.com/etf/qqq/holdings)). That table is nine months old, so treat the weights as *approximate* and have your agent pull current weights from the index provider or an ETF holdings file each week. SpaceX joined on 7 July 2026 at about 1.34% weight under a new Nasdaq rule that lets very large IPOs enter after 15 trading days ([Al Jazeera](https://aljazeera.com/economy/2026/7/7/spacex-shares-slide-as-it-joins-the-tech-heavy-nasdaq-100)).

**What happened on 4 to 6 November 2026 (reported).** It is the best recent example of how this index falls.

1. **Wed 4 Nov:** a strong post-midterm rally (Dow +3%, S&P 500 +1.6% to 7,688.62, oil down more than 8%) ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/11/05/wall-street-drop-off-tech-ai-plunge-2-trillion/)).
2. **Overnight:** Asia sold off hard; South Korea's Kospi fell 5.28% with trading halts.
3. **Thu 5 Nov:** reversal led by chips. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was down about 9.75% intraday, on pace for its worst day since March 2020; Nvidia, AMD and Micron fell hard ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/11/05/wall-street-drop-off-tech-ai-plunge-2-trillion/)). One live report put the Nasdaq-100 down about 6.3%, the worst day since April 2025 ([TheStreet](https://www.thestreet.com/stock-market-today/stock-market-today-dow-jones-sp-500-nasdaq-updates-nov-06-2026)). Media tied it to Democratic midterm wins and ballot measures that threaten data-centre build-out, plus weak chip earnings.
4. **Fri 6 Nov:** a partial rebound, with Nvidia up about 4% before the open and the Nasdaq-100 futures up about 1.3% ([CP24](https://www.cp24.com/news/money/2026/11/06/nasdaq-eyes-higher-open-as-chips-pare-losses-rate-hike-fears-linger/)).

The stated cause is the media's story and may be incomplete. What matters for your system is the mechanism: crowded positions in a few AI stocks, a rate-hike backdrop, and a headline that forced selling in minutes. Statistically, big down days cluster, so a day like 5 November raises the odds of large moves, in both directions, for weeks.

**Earnings.** Companies report four times a year, and the index moves on guidance and spending plans more than on the headline profit. Nvidia is expected to report on **Tue 17 Nov 2026 after the 4:00 pm ET close**, with the first reaction at the next open (date expected, not formally confirmed). Its last four reported moves were -3.2%, -5.5%, -1.8% and +8.7%, and its 12-quarter average move was about 7.4% ([PrimeXBT](https://primexbt.com/for-traders/nvidia-earnings-date/)).

**Agent rules.**

- Refresh index weights weekly; compute the share of the index in the top 3, top 10 and in semiconductors.
- Track the top 10 constituents as separate series. If three or more of them move in the same direction by more than 1.5 times their normal daily range, label the day "narrow mega-cap move" and block mean-reversion trades.
- Block new positions from the close before a top-5 constituent reports until 30 minutes after the next cash open.
- Treat "AI regulation", "data-centre moratorium" and "export controls" headlines as event risk, not as signals.

Professionals do not trade through the big scheduled releases. The spread widens, the first move often reverses, and a stop can be filled far from its price. Your agent should know the calendar and treat each event as a no-entry window.

**Dated calendar, 9 Nov to 24 Dec 2026.** Times are U.S. Eastern (ET, which equals UTC-5 until the clocks change in March) with the UTC and East Africa Time (EAT, UTC+3) equivalents. Dates marked *check* come from lower-quality sources or from the usual pattern, and must be confirmed against the issuer before use.

| Date | Event | Time ET / UTC / EAT | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tue 10 Nov | CPI, October data | 8:30 / 13:30 / 16:30 | [BLS schedule](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/news_release/cpi.htm). Highest-impact in a hiking regime |
| Tue 17 Nov | Nvidia earnings | after 16:00 / 21:00 / 00:00 next day | Expected date, not formally confirmed ([PrimeXBT](https://primexbt.com/for-traders/nvidia-earnings-date/)); reaction at the 18 Nov open |
| about Wed 18 Nov | Minutes of the 28 Oct Fed meeting | 14:00 / 19:00 / 22:00 | *Check*: minutes normally come three weeks after the decision |
| Fri 20 Nov | Monthly options expiry | all day | Third Friday; volume and close can distort |
| Thu 26 Nov | Thanksgiving | cash closed; futures halt 13:00 ET | [QuantVPS](https://www.quantvps.com/blog/nq-mnq-futures-market-hours) |
| Fri 27 Nov | Day after Thanksgiving | early close 13:15 ET | Thin liquidity; avoid |
| Tue 1 Dec | JOLTS (job openings), October | 10:00 / 15:00 / 18:00 | [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/2026/12_sched_list.htm) |
| Fri 4 Dec | Jobs report, November | 8:30 / 13:30 / 16:30 | [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/2026/12_sched_list.htm) |
| Wed 9 Dec | **Fed decision** and press conference | 14:00 / 19:00 / 22:00 | [Calendar](https://therighttrader.com/economic-calendar/fomc); a hike was priced at about 78% on 6 Nov |
| Thu 10 Dec | CPI, November data | 8:30 / 13:30 / 16:30 | [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/2026/12_sched_list.htm); the day after the Fed |
| Tue 15 Dec | Producer prices, November | 8:30 / 13:30 / 16:30 | [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/2026/12_sched_list.htm) |
| Fri 18 Dec | Quarterly options and futures expiry | all day | Third Friday of December |
| Mon 21 Dec | Nasdaq-100 annual reconstitution takes effect | at the open | [Nasdaq methodology](https://indexes.nasdaqomx.com/docs/methodology_NDX.pdf); announcement usually early December (*check*) |
| Thu 24 Dec | Christmas Eve | futures close 13:15 ET | [QuantVPS](https://www.quantvps.com/blog/nq-mnq-futures-market-hours) |
| Fri 25 Dec | Christmas Day | closed |  |

Not verified in this research: retail sales (Census), the PCE inflation measure (BEA), Treasury refunding and auctions, and other Fed speakers. Add them from the official calendars. Also unscheduled and undated: Iran war and Strait of Hormuz headlines, tariff and export-control news, and AI-regulation announcements.

**Event tiers and what to do (convention, tune in testing).**

| Tier | Examples | No new entries | Resume when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Fed decision, CPI, jobs report, Nvidia earnings reaction | 30 minutes before to 30 minutes after (Fed: 13:30 ET until 30 minutes after the press conference begins) | Spread back under 1.5 times its 20-day median and the first 5-minute range is complete |
| 2 | PPI, JOLTS, Fed minutes, retail sales, other top-5 earnings | 15 minutes before to 15 minutes after | Spread normal |
| 3 | Monthly expiry, quarter-end, index rebalance days | Allowed with half size | Not applicable |
| Holiday | Early closes, day after Thanksgiving, Christmas week | No new trades | Normal session |

**Open positions through an event.** The safest rule for a first system is none: flat before tier 1, or a stop that is placed and tested for a gap of several times the average range. Never widen or remove a stop because an event is near.

**Agent rules.** Load the calendar from official sources into a table with release time in UTC. Compute `minutes_to_next_event` and `minutes_since_last_event` for every bar. Before each event, if the spread is above its threshold the answer is NO TRADE with the reason code `EVENT_WINDOW`.

sections.section: 6. Sessions, time zones and when liquidity is real
sections.text:
Most of the index's real trading and most of its meaningful moves happen between the U.S. cash open at 9:30 am ET and the close at 4:00 pm ET. Outside those hours the market trades on futures only, with thinner volume and wider spreads, so setups there are less reliable.

**Session map (winter clocks, 1 Nov 2026 to early Mar 2027).**

| Session | ET | UTC | EAT (Nairobi) | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Asia | 19:00 to 01:00 | 00:00 to 06:00 | 03:00 to 09:00 | Mostly range; reacts to Asian chip stocks (Korea, Taiwan, Japan) |
| London | 03:00 to 11:30 | 08:00 to 16:30 | 11:00 to 19:30 | Sets the overnight range; liquidity builds toward the U.S. open |
| U.S. pre-open | 08:30 | 13:30 | 16:30 | Scheduled data releases land here |
| **U.S. cash open** | **09:30** | **14:30** | **17:30** | Largest volume and volatility of the day; opening gap resolves here |
| London / New York overlap | 09:30 to 11:30 | 14:30 to 16:30 | 17:30 to 19:30 | Deepest liquidity for the index |
| Lunch lull | about 11:30 to 14:00 | about 16:30 to 19:00 | about 19:30 to 22:00 | Narrower ranges, more false breakouts (*convention*) |
| Fed hour | 14:00 on decision days | 19:00 | 22:00 | Statement at 14:00, press conference 14:30 |
| **U.S. cash close** | **16:00** | **21:00** | **00:00** | Closing auction flows; futures keep trading |
| Futures daily break | 17:00 to 18:00 | 22:00 to 23:00 | 01:00 to 02:00 | No futures trading; your broker's quote may freeze or widen |

Futures run Sunday 6:00 pm ET to Friday 5:00 pm ET with that one-hour break ([QuantVPS](https://www.quantvps.com/blog/nq-mnq-futures-market-hours)). EAT never changes, so the same New York time falls an hour earlier on your clock in summer. Session boundaries above are the common convention; confirm the hours of your own broker's symbol.

**The daylight-saving trap.** The United States and Europe change clocks on different dates. In 2026 the U.S. went to summer time on 8 Mar and back on 1 Nov; Europe went on 29 Mar and back on 25 Oct. For the weeks between (about 8 to 29 March and 25 Oct to 1 Nov) the gap between London and New York is one hour different from the rest of the year. Your own earlier captures suggest the broker's bar labels follow European summer time rather than UTC (see the NAS100 handover report, section 5.2b). That is a hypothesis until measured. A wrong offset moves the "New York open" by an hour, which silently ruins every session rule in this document. The agent must convert timestamps with a verified rule before computing any session feature.

**Typical intraday behaviour (convention, supported by research, not a guarantee).**

- Volume and volatility are highest at the open and into the close, with a quieter middle of the day.
- Gao, Han, Li and Zhou (published 2018) found that on the S&P 500 ETF from 1999 to 2012 the first half-hour return predicted the last half-hour return, but explained only about 2% of its variance, and the summary does not say whether the strategy survives costs or after 2012 ([Alpha Architect summary](https://alphaarchitect.com/2014/08/attention-prop-traders-the-first-half-hour-of-trading-predicts-the-last-half-hour/)).
- A vendor's six-month study of Nasdaq futures to February 2026 (127 days, method not fully stated) reported: the 15-minute opening range broke on one side on most days, but both sides broke on about 30% of days; full gap fill happened on 53% of gap-ups and 59% of gap-downs; Thursday and Friday ranges were larger than Monday and Tuesday ([edgeful](https://www.edgeful.com/blog/posts/nq-futures-trading)). Treat those as ideas to test on your own data, not as facts about the market.

**Hypotheses to test, not rules to trust.**

1. No entries in the first 5 to 15 minutes after the cash open, when spread and slippage are worst.
2. Highest-quality window is 09:45 to 11:30 ET; secondary window 14:00 to 15:30 ET on non-event days.
3. Avoid the last 10 minutes before the daily break and the broker's rollover time.

**Agent rules.** Compute `session`, `minutes_since_cash_open`, `minutes_to_cash_close`, `is_us_dst`, `is_eu_dst` and `dst_mismatch_week` from verified UTC timestamps. Never use broker server time directly for session logic.

Professionals use price levels and structure to decide where to act, not whether to act. Whether to act comes from sections 3 to 6 and 8. A level or pattern is only a place to look for entry and a place to put a stop.

**What the evidence says.** I found no rigorous, independent study showing that ICT-style patterns (fair value gaps, order blocks, liquidity sweeps, premium and discount) earn money after costs on the Nasdaq-100. They are a vocabulary of price behaviour, so they are *convention* until your own tests show otherwise. The wider literature is a warning: a study of more than 28,000 technical rules on Chinese stock data found fewer than 1% showed real skill after correcting for data snooping ([Alpha Architect summary](https://alphaarchitect.com/technical-trading-rules-data-snooping-evidence-china/); a different market and period, but the same statistical trap). Counting more confluences does not by itself raise the odds; it may only shrink the sample.

**Levels professionals mark every day.**

| Level | Definition the agent can compute | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prior day high, low, close | From the 09:30 to 16:00 ET cash session | Most-watched references; stops cluster beyond them |
| Overnight high and low | From 18:00 ET (futures open) to 09:30 ET | Defines the range the U.S. open will probe |
| Opening range | High and low of the first 5, 15 or 30 minutes after 09:30 ET | Breakout or failure of it is a common intraday trigger |
| Session VWAP | Volume-weighted average price since 09:30 ET (needs futures volume; CFD tick volume is a weak substitute) | Acts as fair value; trend days hold one side |
| Weekly and monthly open, high, low | Calendar-based | Higher-timeframe reference |
| Round numbers | Every 500 and 1,000 index points | Orders and options strikes cluster there |
| Gap | Today's open minus yesterday's cash close | Often partly retraced; direction of the gap in a macro shock matters more than its size |

**Structure concepts (defined so code can detect them).**

- **Swing high or low.** A bar whose high (low) is the highest (lowest) of `n` bars on each side. It is only known `n` bars later, so signals must be stamped at confirmation time, not at the swing bar.
- **Higher highs and higher lows** mean an uptrend; the reverse means a downtrend. Do it on at least two timeframes, for example 15 minutes and 4 hours.
- **Break of structure (BOS).** A candle close beyond the last swing in the trend direction. **Change of character (CHoCH).** A close beyond the last swing against the trend. Use closes, not wicks, or the signal fires on every spike.
- **Liquidity sweep.** Price trades through a prior high or low (stops sit there) and closes back inside within a few bars. The classic reversal clue, but only informative with context.
- **Displacement.** A large-range candle or run (for example, range above 1.5 times the 14-bar ATR) that breaks structure.
- **Fair value gap (FVG).** Three candles where the first candle's high is below the third candle's low (bullish gap) or the reverse. The gap is "open" until price trades back through it.
- **Order block.** The last opposite-coloured candle before a displacement. Hard to define without discretion, so test it last.
- **Premium and discount.** Whether price is in the upper or lower half of a defined range (for example, the range between the last confirmed swing high and low). Used to prefer buying low and selling high within a range.
- **Invalidation.** The price that proves the idea wrong, for example the low of the sweep for a long. A setup with no clean invalidation is not a setup.

Your repository's NAS100 engine already implements swings, BOS and CHoCH, FVGs, sweeps and a checklist-style decision chain with look-ahead protection. This section is the knowledge behind it; its numbers still need research-grade data to test.

**A scoring idea that is testable.** Give each candidate setup a score from 0 to 1 using at most five features (higher-timeframe trend agreement, sweep present, displacement present, FVG retraced to its midpoint, risk-to-reward at least 1.5). Then test, out of sample and after costs, whether score bands actually separate outcomes. If they do not, delete the score. If they do, it is a feature for the filter stack, not a decision.

**Agent rules.**

- Every level and pattern gets `detected_at` (the time it became knowable) and is never used earlier.
- Setups are rejected if the stop distance is smaller than the current spread multiplied by 5, or larger than 2 times the daily ATR.
- Record every rejected and every taken setup with the reason, so the sample is not biased toward winners.

The same setup behaves differently in a calm market and a stressed one, so the first filter is the regime. Volatility clusters: after a shock like 5 November, large moves in both directions are more likely for days to weeks, and stops that were adequate last month are too tight.

**Measures to compute and store.**

- **Realised volatility and ATR percentile.** The 14-bar ATR and the 20-day realised volatility, each ranked against the previous 250 trading days. This is the primary regime variable because you can compute it from your own data.
- **Implied volatility.** The VIX is the S&P 500's 30-day implied volatility; it stood at 26.70 on 6 Nov after its biggest one-day jump in about 19 months ([CP24](https://www.cp24.com/news/money/2026/11/06/nasdaq-eyes-higher-open-as-chips-pare-losses-rate-hike-fears-linger/)). The Nasdaq-100 has its own, the VXN, which measures expected volatility over 30 days from Nasdaq-100 options ([Fidelity](https://fidelity.com/learning-center/trading-investing/technical-analysis/technical-indicator-guide/cboe-nasdaq-vxn)). I did not find a reliable VXN level for 6 Nov.
- **Trend versus range.** Kaufman efficiency ratio (net move divided by total path over `n` bars) on the 15-minute and hourly charts. Near 1 means trending; near 0 means choppy.
- **Breadth.** Share of the 100 stocks above their 50-day average, and the ratio of the equal-weight Nasdaq-100 to the cap-weighted one. When the index rises while breadth falls, the rally depends on a few names (section 4).
- **Gap and range expansion.** Today's range divided by the 20-day average range. Above 2 is an expansion day.

**Options positioning (context, not a signal).** Options expiring the same day (0DTE) were reported at up to 60% of S&P 500 options volume in early 2026 ([SpotGamma](https://spotgamma.com/record-0dte-volume-reshapes-the-sp-500/)). The standard idea is that when dealers are net long options they sell rallies and buy dips, which calms trading; when they are net short they chase moves, which amplifies them. You cannot see dealer positioning directly, only estimates from vendors, so use it as a reason to widen caution near large option strikes, not as a trade trigger.

**Regime table. The numbers are starting values to test, not proven thresholds.**

| Regime | How to detect | Allowed behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calm | ATR and realised vol below the 40th percentile, VIX below 16 | Normal size; range tactics allowed; watch for sudden expansion |
| Normal | 40th to 75th percentile, VIX 16 to 22 | Normal rules |
| Elevated | 75th to 90th percentile, or VIX 22 to 30 | Half size, wider stops, no range fading near highs and lows of the day |
| Stress | Above the 90th percentile, or VIX above 30, or a daily move beyond 4% in the last 5 days | NO TRADE by default; if allowed, a quarter of normal size, trend direction only, no entry in the first hour |
| Post-shock | Within 10 trading days of a daily move beyond 4% | Treated as one level worse than the measured regime |

As of 6 Nov 2026 the evidence points to *Elevated* at least and probably *Post-shock* (a reported daily fall of about 6% on 5 Nov). Your agent should compute this itself from your data and not trust this paragraph.

**Agent rules.** Position size is set from volatility (section 12), so risk in money stays constant while the distance to the stop grows. The regime also gates the entry window and the maximum number of trades per day.

The index rarely moves alone. A move in Nasdaq futures that other markets do not confirm is weaker, and a move other markets lead is easier to read. Use these as context and filters; none is a trigger by itself.

**The yield relationship is not constant.** Nasdaq's own research (November 2021, monthly data from 1985) found that when the 10-year yield was low, equities tended to rise along with yields, but when yields were above about 5%, further rises tended to hurt equities, with the Nasdaq-100 most sensitive of the three indices studied ([Nasdaq Investment Intelligence](https://indexes.NASDAQomx.com/docs/Interest%20rate%20sensitivity%20of%20the%20Nasdaq-100.pdf)). The paper itself has inconsistent tables, rests on few high-yield observations and uses yields as a proxy for the Fed, so treat it as a reason for caution, not a law. With the 10-year near 5% today, that is the regime where rising yields are the more dangerous direction.

| Signal | Usual relation to the index | What the 2026 evidence shows | How the agent uses it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10-year Treasury yield | Rising yields pressure growth stocks | Near 5%; a stronger jobs report on 6 Nov lifted hike odds from 70% to 78% as tech sold off | Block new longs when the 10-year rises more than 10 basis points in a day (starting value) |
| Fed hike probability (futures-implied) | Higher odds, lower index in this regime | 78% for 9 Dec on 6 Nov | Daily input; a jump of 10 points in a day marks a regime change day |
| Oil | In an inflation scare, oil up means index down | Oil fell more than 8% on 4 Nov as stocks rallied; a crude jump on 5 Nov stoked rate fears ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/11/05/wall-street-drop-off-tech-ai-plunge-2-trillion/), [CP24](https://www.cp24.com/news/money/2026/11/06/nasdaq-eyes-higher-open-as-chips-pare-losses-rate-hike-fears-linger/)) | Treat a daily oil move beyond 4% as an event window for the day |
| U.S. dollar index | Strong dollar pressures mega-cap overseas revenue | Not researched | Optional trend filter |
| Semiconductor index | Leads the Nasdaq-100 in an AI-driven market | Fell about 9.75% intraday on 5 Nov; AI power and data-centre names (Vistra, Vertiv) had already fallen 13% to 14% on 4 Nov, a day before the chip rout | If semis fall more than 2 times their ATR while the index holds, treat the index as vulnerable |
| S&P 500, Dow, Russell 2000 | Confirmation and rotation | On 6 Nov at the open the Nasdaq was up about 1% while the Dow was down about 1%, a sign of rotation ([TheStreet](https://www.thestreet.com/stock-market-today/stock-market-today-dow-jones-sp-500-nasdaq-updates-nov-06-2026)) | Require index and S&P 500 futures to agree on direction for trend entries |
| VIX and VXN | Spike means risk-off | Biggest one-day VIX jump in about 19 months on 5 Nov | Section 8 regime table |
| Asian chip markets (Korea, Taiwan, Japan) | Overnight lead for semiconductors | Kospi fell 5.28% with halts before the 5 Nov U.S. open ([Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/11/05/wall-street-drop-off-tech-ai-plunge-2-trillion/)) | Overnight gap risk flag for the next U.S. open |
| Bitcoin | Trades 24 hours and weekends; a sentiment gauge | Fell 4.57% to about $75,950 on 6 Nov ([TheStreet](https://www.thestreet.com/stock-market-today/stock-market-today-dow-jones-sp-500-nasdaq-updates-nov-06-2026)) | Weekend risk-appetite check before the Sunday open |

**Correlations shift, so measure them.** Compute the 20-day rolling correlation of the index with each series each day. When a usual relationship flips sign for several days, the regime has changed and your rules from the old regime should not be trusted.

**Agent rules.** Pull each series at the same timestamps as the index bars and keep a daily snapshot. A cross-asset filter can only block or reduce a trade. It must never be the reason to open one.

Declines of 10% to 15% happen almost every year, and deeper ones come when rising rates, a crowded theme and a shock arrive together. Knowing the pattern helps the agent stay out, which is where most of a professional's edge comes from.

**How often it falls.** Using ChartRow's estimates of the deepest peak-to-trough fall inside each calendar year from 2000 to 2026 (QQQ as a proxy for the index, so approximate; [ChartRow](https://chartrow.com/nasdaq-100/year-by-year)), I counted: 24 of 27 years had a fall of at least 10%, 13 of 27 had at least 15%, 8 had at least 20%, and 5 had at least 30%. The median year's worst fall was 14.8%. In 2026 the fall so far is 14.8% (6 Oct to 5 Nov), which is an ordinary-sized fall by that measure, and history says it can go much deeper.

| Year | Window | Deepest fall | Context (general knowledge, not from ChartRow) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2000 | 27 Mar to 20 Dec | -52.7% | Dot-com bubble burst after rate rises |
| 2008 | 31 Dec 2007 to 20 Nov | -50.1% | Financial crisis |
| 2018 | 29 Aug to 24 Dec | -22.8% | Fed hikes and balance-sheet reduction, trade-war fears |
| 2020 | 19 Feb to 16 Mar | -28.6% | Pandemic; fastest fall on the list, then a fast recovery |
| 2022 | 3 Jan to 3 Nov | -34.8% | Inflation and the Fed's hiking cycle |
| 2025 | 19 Feb to 8 Apr | -22.8% | Tariff shock |
| 2026 | 6 Oct to 5 Nov (so far) | -14.8% | Rate-hike expectations, oil shock, AI selloff (section 4) |

**What the declines have in common (convention; each point must be tested).**

1. **Rising yields or a hawkish repricing of the Fed** came before 2000, 2018 and 2022, and is present now.
2. **Narrow, crowded leadership.** A few stocks carrying the index means one theme's reversal hits everything (section 4).
3. **A catalyst that forces selling.** Policy, geopolitics or an earnings miss in a leader.
4. **Breadth and trend deterioration first.** Weekly losses in a row, lower highs, the index below its 50-day and 200-day averages. The Nasdaq was headed for a fourth straight weekly loss as of 6 Nov ([CP24](https://www.cp24.com/news/money/2026/11/06/nasdaq-eyes-higher-open-as-chips-pare-losses-rate-hike-fears-linger/)).
5. **Volatility expansion.** The VIX jumping and staying high, and daily ranges doubling.

**What it looks like once it starts.**

- **Rallies are violent and short.** 4 Nov rose, 5 Nov fell about 6%, 6 Nov rebounded within a day. In a falling market a 3% to 5% bounce is common and does not mean the fall is over.
- **Gaps replace candles.** The first move often happens while your broker is closed or thin, so a stop may fill far beyond its price.
- **Correlations go to one.** Everything the index holds falls together, so diversification inside it does not help.
- **Support and resistance levels break more often.** Retests are sharper and wicks longer, so structure signals that worked in calm weeks produce more false entries.

**What professionals do.** Reduce size before the decline (when yields and breadth warn), trade smaller with wider stops during it, avoid fading the first two or three days of a large move, and wait for volatility to settle and for a higher low to confirm before leaning long again. None of this guarantees a better result; it limits the chance of the damage that ends accounts.

**Agent rules.** Compute `drawdown_from_52w_high`, `consecutive_down_weeks`, `index_vs_50d_and_200d`, `breadth_above_50d`, `top10_share_change_20d` and `ten_year_change_20d` daily. Combine them into a `fragility_score` from 0 to 5 (one point each for: 10-year yield up over 20 days; top-10 share up over 20 days; index below both its 50-day and 200-day averages; three or more down weeks in a row; ATR percentile above 75; all starting values). At 3 or more, apply the Elevated rules of section 8 even if measured volatility looks normal.

The answer is NO TRADE unless every gate below passes, checked in this order, cheapest and most decisive first. The first failing gate ends the check and its reason code is logged. Entry rules come at gate 8, which is why most of the work happens before any chart pattern.

1. **Data is trustworthy.** Timebase verified, last bar is closed and fresh, no unexplained gaps, feed alive, clock within tolerance. Fail: `DATA_INVALID`, `TIMEBASE_UNVERIFIED`, `STALE_DATA`.
2. **Account and permission.** Owner has enabled the mode; daily and total loss limits not hit; trade count below the day's cap; no kill switch set. Fail: `LOSS_LIMIT`, `MAX_TRADES`, `KILL_SWITCH`, `MODE_DISABLED`.
3. **Calendar.** Not inside a tier 1 or tier 2 window, not a holiday or early close (section 5). Fail: `EVENT_WINDOW`, `HOLIDAY`.
4. **Session.** Inside an allowed window and not in the first minutes after the cash open or near the daily break (section 6). Fail: `OUT_OF_SESSION`.
5. **Cost.** Current spread at most 1.5 times its 20-day median for this hour, and the stop distance at least 5 times the spread. Fail: `SPREAD_WIDE`, `STOP_TOO_TIGHT`.
6. **Regime.** Volatility regime and fragility score allow trading (sections 8 and 10). Stress means stop. Fail: `REGIME_STRESS`, `POST_SHOCK`.
7. **Context.** Cross-asset filters do not contradict the direction (section 9); the higher-timeframe trend and the next major level agree or the trade is a pure range play with a defined edge. Fail: `CROSS_ASSET_CONFLICT`, `HTF_CONFLICT`.
8. **Setup.** The ordered chain is complete: liquidity sweep or level test, then a structure shift with displacement, then a retrace into an open gap or level, then a trigger candle close. Invalidation price defined. Fail: `NO_SETUP`, `SETUP_INCOMPLETE`.
9. **Geometry and risk.** Entry, stop and target defined; reward-to-risk at least 1.5 after spread, slippage and commission; position size computed from risk per trade (section 12) and not below the broker's minimum lot. Fail: `BAD_GEOMETRY`, `RR_TOO_LOW`, `SIZE_BELOW_MIN`.
10. **Concurrency.** No open position in the same direction or an unresolved previous order. Fail: `POSITION_OPEN`.
11. **Output.** BUY or SELL with entry, stop, target, invalidation, size, confidence label (only if a calibrated model exists) and the full list of reasons. Always labelled "research signal" until the owner approves execution.

**After entry.** The stop is never widened. Close if invalidation is hit, at the time stop, ahead of a tier 1 event, or when the daily loss limit is reached. The decision engine and the execution layer are separate: a signal is a message; an order needs a human-approved mode.

**Why this order works.** Gates 1 to 7 reject most bars cheaply and with no price pattern at all. The pattern in gate 8 then only has to be right in the situations where trading is allowed, which is how professionals keep their sample small, clean and testable.

**Agent rules.** Return the structure `{decision, reasons[], failed_gate, inputs_snapshot, timestamp_utc}` for every bar, including NO TRADE. Log them. A NO TRADE with a clear code is a valid, valuable output, and you will study these logs more than the trades.

Survival rules decide whether any edge gets the time to show up. Most retail CFD traders lose: broker disclosures put the share of losing retail accounts at about 68% to 81% at five large brokers, and the article reporting them says the UK regulator has stated that about 80% of CFD customers lose money ([Pound Sterling Live, 27 Mar 2026](https://www.poundsterlinglive.com/news/23132-even-at-major-uk-brokers-most-cfd-accounts-lost-money-report-finds)). Those are account loss rates, not a verdict on any system, but they are the base rate you are trying to beat.

**Limits to set before the first real trade.** Values are starting points for a first live phase; tighten rather than loosen them.

| Control | Starting value | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Risk per trade | 0.25% to 0.5% of equity | A 20-trade losing streak is normal for any system; this survives it |
| Daily loss limit | 1.5% of equity, then stop until the next day | Prevents revenge trading and gap-day spirals |
| Weekly loss limit | 3% | Forces a review |
| Drawdown halt | 6% from the equity peak | Stop, review the log, return to demo |
| Trades per day | At most 2 | Keeps the sample clean and the costs low |
| Open positions | 1 | Index positions are one correlated bet |
| Gap stress | Risk per trade × 3 must be below the daily loss limit | A stop is not a guarantee; the index fell about 6% in a day on 5 Nov |
| Notional exposure | At most 3 times equity | A 6% adverse day on 3 times leverage costs 18% of equity even when everything works |
| Cost budget | Spread + slippage + commission under 15% of the stop distance | Costs are a certain loss on every trade |
| Averaging down, martingale | Never | Turns a small loss into an account-ending one |
| Stop order | Placed with the order, never widened, never removed |  |

**Position size from the stop, not from a feeling.**

```latex
\text{lots} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{equity} \times r}{\text{stop distance (points)} \times \text{value per point per lot}} \right\rfloor_{\text{volume step}}
```

Here `r` is the risk fraction. Value per point comes from the broker's contract specification for your own symbol (tick value, tick size, point size, minimum lot, lot step, currency), read from the terminal. If any field is missing or the size is below the minimum lot, the answer is NO TRADE, not a rounded-up size. Your existing gateway already sizes this way and fails closed when contract data is missing; keep it that way.

**Keep the existing risk formula.** The project's infrastructure-adjusted ceiling, `Effective = Base × (1 − 0.5 × Stress / 100)`, stays unchanged. The regime multipliers in section 8 apply on top and can only reduce size.

**Funded or prop accounts.** Each firm sets its own daily loss limit, maximum drawdown, news-trading rules, weekend-holding rules and consistency rules, and they differ. I did not research any firm's current rules. Load yours into the compliance engine as data, and set your internal limits at no more than half of the firm's, so a gap day does not breach an external limit.

**Scaling up with real money.** Move in stages: demo with the full agent, then the smallest live size, then larger only after a fixed number of trades (for example 100) in which net expectancy after all costs is positive with a lower confidence bound above zero. Never raise size because of a winning streak, and drop back one stage after a drawdown halt.

**Agent rules.** Compute and log every limit as a number before each decision. Breaching any limit sets a `KILL_SWITCH` flag that only the owner can clear.

You trade your broker's quote, not the index, so the broker's costs and rules are part of the strategy. A setup that works on index data can lose after the spread, the swap and a stop that fills late.

**Cost items and how the agent should handle each.**

| Item | What it is | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spread | Ask minus bid; changes by the hour and widens at the open, near events and in stress | Record the spread of every bar (your exports already carry `spread_points`) and compare each entry to the median for that hour |
| Slippage | Difference between the price you wanted and the price you got | Cannot be measured on a demo account, whose fills are usually idealised. Use a stress scenario (for example, 2 to 5 index points each side, more near events) until you have live fills |
| Commission | A fee per lot, on some account types | Read from the account terms; include in every backtest |
| Swap (overnight financing) | Charged on positions held past the daily rollover, often around 5:00 pm New York time; usually three days' worth on Wednesday ([Afterprime](https://afterprime.com/glossary/overnight-financing)) | Read `swap_mode`, `swap_long`, `swap_short` and `swap_rollover3days` from the symbol; check the sign yourself because direction differs by broker |
| Gaps | Price jumps while the broker is closed or thin | A stop is filled at the next available price, which can be far past it; see the gap stress rule in section 12 |
| Stop level | Minimum distance the broker allows between price and a stop | Read `trade_stops_level` and `trade_freeze_level`; reject setups tighter than that |
| Minimum lot and step | `volume_min`, `volume_step` | Position size cannot be smaller than this, so a small account may be unable to risk 0.25% on a wide stop |

**Swap detail worth knowing.** On MetaTrader 5, index swaps are quoted in several ways, for example a fixed number of points per night or an annual percentage of price, and the mode is set by `SYMBOL_SWAP_MODE`. Brokers also change swap values with no notice, so a snapshot taken once is wrong later ([MQL5 article on swaps](https://www.mql5.com/en/articles/23469)). Log a dated snapshot of the specification every day. A strategy that holds positions overnight should model swap from the logged history, not from today's number.

**Things specific to your setup (from the earlier audit).**

- Your broker symbol `USTECH100M` was reported as trade-disabled on the MetaQuotes demo server, so quotes and history can be studied, but fills, spread behaviour and swaps there may not represent a live tradable symbol. Confirm the live symbol, its hours and costs before any real money.
- Contract specifications captured from a terminal are current values, not history. Date every snapshot.
- Broker history for minute data may be shorter than you need and may have gaps; measure the real depth before planning any training.
- Broker bar timestamps must be converted with a measured rule (section 6) before any session logic.
- A demo or investor-password connection for data is a read-only job. Trading permissions must never be switched on to make an export work.

**Execution notes.**

- Use limit or stop orders with an expiry, not market orders in fast conditions.
- Place the stop and target with the order. Never leave a position without a stop, even for a moment.
- Check the spread again at the moment of sending; if it has doubled since the decision, cancel.
- Do not trade the minute around the daily break and rollover, when quotes can freeze or widen.

**Agent rules.** Build a `broker_profile` file per symbol with dated fields: tick value, tick size, point, contract size, volume limits, stop level, swap mode and values, session hours, commission. The decision engine refuses to run if the profile is older than 24 hours or any field is missing.

sections.section: 14. Extra NO TRADE conditions and common mistakes
sections.text:
Beyond the gates in section 11, a professional also stands aside in the situations below. Each becomes a reason code the agent can log and count.

**Add these to the NO TRADE list.**

- Any required input is missing or unknown (spread, calendar, regime, higher-timeframe state). Unknown means no. `UNKNOWN_INPUT`
- Two consecutive losses today, or the day's loss is above half the daily limit. `DAY_DEGRADED`
- Friday after 15:00 ET with the intention to hold over the weekend, or any position that would be open at the daily break. `WEEKEND_RISK`
- Timeframes disagree and no range edge is defined. `TF_CONFLICT`
- The signal depends on a model that is missing, stale, uncalibrated or built on a different feature set. `MODEL_UNAVAILABLE`
- A tier 1 event, an Iran or Hormuz headline, a regulatory announcement or a top-5 constituent's guidance cut happened in the last 30 minutes and the spread has not normalised. `NEWS_SHOCK`
- The system has just been changed (new rule, new data, new parameters) and has not completed a demo period. `UNVALIDATED_CHANGE`

**Mistakes experienced traders say they see most (convention; they match the failure modes in the evidence above).**

1. **Trading through scheduled events** because the move looks obvious. It usually reverses and fills badly.
2. **Moving or removing a stop** to avoid being wrong.
3. **Overtrading** after a loss or a boring morning; costs and mistakes compound.
4. **Ignoring costs** in the plan, so a small edge turns negative.
5. **Fitting the past.** Tuning rules until the history looks great; the Chinese rules study found fewer than 1% of 28,000 rules survived honest testing (section 7).
6. **One strategy for every regime.** A breakout rule in a range, or a dip-buy in a falling market.
7. **Treating the index as several independent trades** when open positions are all the same bet.
8. **Using too much leverage**, so a normal bad day becomes a margin call.
9. **Raising size after wins** and calling it confidence.
10. **Believing a backtest is proof.** It is a filter for bad ideas, not evidence of a good one.

**Agent rules.** Count how often each reason code fires per week and print the table. If one code fires more than 70% of the time, either the market is telling you something or your threshold is mis-set, and the owner should look at it.

sections.section: 15. Implementation spec for the code agent
sections.text:
Build the decision engine as a chain of gates (section 11) fed by a daily regime snapshot and a per-bar feature table, with every threshold in a versioned configuration file. Every number in this document marked "starting value" lives in that file, never in code. This extends your existing `backend/nas100` engine; it does not replace it.

**Data inputs.**

| Input | Source | Frequency | Alignment rule |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NAS100 bars M1 to D1 | MT5 read-only history calls, after the timebase is verified | per bar | Use closed bars only; convert to UTC with the measured rule |
| Spread and contract profile | MT5 symbol specification, dated snapshot | daily and per bar | Engine refuses stale or incomplete profiles |
| Event calendar | Official pages: [BLS](https://www.bls.gov/schedule/2026/12_sched_list.htm), the Fed's FOMC calendar, BEA (PCE), Census (retail sales), company investor-relations pages | monthly refresh, weekly check | Store `release_time_utc`; rebuild after any change |
| Index weights | Nasdaq or an ETF holdings file | weekly | As-of date stored; never back-filled |
| 10-year and real 10-year yield | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/DFII10) series DGS10 and DFII10 (confirm IDs) | daily, published after the close | Usable only from the next session; intraday needs a different feed |
| VIX and VXN | Cboe history | daily | Same next-session rule for daily closes |
| Fed hike odds | CME FedWatch (check licence; may be manual entry) | daily | Record the time of the reading |
| Cross-assets (S&P 500, Dow, semis, dollar, oil) | Broker symbols if offered, otherwise skip | per bar | Same timestamps as the index |

Free daily series arrive with a delay. Join them to bars with an *as-of* join using the time the value became public, or the system will use information it could not have had.

**Feature groups (all computed from data available at the decision time).**

- Price and structure: swings, BOS and CHoCH, sweep flags, displacement, open FVGs, distance to prior-day, overnight and opening-range levels, premium or discount.
- Volatility and regime: ATR and realised-volatility percentiles, efficiency ratio, range expansion, `fragility_score`.
- Time: session, minutes since cash open and to close, minutes to and since the next and last event, DST flags.
- Cost: spread over its hourly median, stop distance over spread, swap.
- Context: 10-year yield change, hike-probability change, oil change, semiconductor move, S&P 500 agreement, breadth, top-10 share.

**Output for every bar, including NO TRADE.**

```json
{
  "timestamp_utc": "2026-11-10T13:45:00Z",
  "decision": "NO_TRADE",
  "failed_gate": 3,
  "reasons": ["EVENT_WINDOW"],
  "regime": "post_shock",
  "fragility_score": 3,
  "inputs_hash": "sha256 of the exact inputs used",
  "config_version": "2026-11-06.1",
  "label": "RESEARCH_SIGNAL_NOT_EXECUTION"
}
```

**Build order, each step finished and tested before the next.**

1. Timebase verification and UTC conversion, then the event calendar and DST utilities. Acceptance: tests on 8 Mar, 29 Mar, 25 Oct and 1 Nov 2026.
2. Broker profile and cost gate. Acceptance: missing field gives NO TRADE.
3. Regime snapshot and fragility score, computed from stored history.
4. Gate chain with reason codes and logging; run it on history in replay mode with no setup logic at all and look at how often each gate blocks.
5. Setup detection (your existing engine) behind gate 8, with `detected_at` stamping.
6. Backtest and event study after costs, then demo trading in replay and live paper mode, then the validation steps in the training roadmap.
7. Only then: an optional model as a filter after the gates, per the training roadmap.

**Tests that must exist.**

- No look-ahead: features computed on a prefix equal the same features computed on the full series.
- Calendar and DST edge cases, including holidays and early closes.
- Every reason code has a test that triggers it.
- Replay of 5 Nov 2026, 4 to 6 Nov in full, and of April 2025 and March 2020 once data exists. Expected: Stress and Post-shock gates block entries, and the log shows why.
- A kill-switch test: breaching a limit makes every later decision NO TRADE until the owner clears it.

**The AI's role.** After gates 1 to 7 and a valid setup, a model may only veto or downgrade a trade. It never creates a trade the rules did not propose, and a missing or uncalibrated model means "rules only", not "model says go". See `NAS100_AI_RESEARCH_AND_TRAINING_ROADMAP.md` for the data, validation and acceptance steps.

sections.section: 16. Validation and the limits of this document
sections.text:
Nothing here proves a trading edge. It describes how professionals frame the market, and it turns that framing into rules you can test. Real money should only follow evidence from your own tests.

**What is solid.** The index construction and rebalancing rules, the trading hours, the dated calendar (apart from items marked *check*), the structure of the macro regime and the historical frequency of large declines. These are from official or well-documented sources and can be confirmed.

**What is reported but unconfirmed.** the market moves of 4 to 6 November 2026 come from live blogs and news summaries whose figures differ in places (for example, the unemployment rate was reported as 4.1% in one passage and forecast at 4.2% in another, and the payroll figures given for the previous month differ between outlets). The explanations offered (midterm results, AI regulation) are the media's narrative. Confirm index levels and closes against an official data source before using them in code.

**What is convention or hypothesis.** The session windows, every threshold in the regime and risk tables, the FVG, order-block and sweep ideas, the intraday statistics, and the cross-asset relationships. Each must be tested on a dataset that passes the integrity checks in the handover documents, with costs, out-of-sample and with a record of how many variants were tried.

**What was not researched.**

- Your broker's live contract specification, spread history, swap values and exact trading hours.
- Any prop firm's current rules.
- The dollar index, retail sales and PCE dates, and options-dealer positioning data.
- Tax, regulation and the legal position of CFD trading where you live.
- A VXN level and the current index weights.

**Honest expectations.**

- The most likely outcome of careful testing is a small edge, or none, concentrated in a few conditions. That outcome is still useful: it tells you when not to trade.
- A system that trades rarely and stands aside most days can still lose; its advantage is that it does not lose fast.
- Retail loss rates are high (section 12) and a first live period will contain losing streaks that are normal, not signs of failure or success.
- This is research and education, not financial advice. I am not a licensed adviser. Decisions about real money, and any tax or legal questions, are yours and your advisers'.

**Suggested next steps for you.** Run the data and timebase tasks from the handover roadmap first, then the gate chain in replay (section 15, step 4), and only then decide whether to test a setup or a model.
